transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2027-11-10 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Ravi Shah (Redwood SE), Dr. Maya Chen, Omar Ruiz, Priya Patel (Nebula Analytics)

Summary:
Quick technical review focused on quantization strategies for Nebula's inference workloads. Discussed tradeoffs between INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ, accuracy regressions, runtime implications (latency/throughput), KV cache interaction, batching strategies, and VPC/on-prem deployment concerns. Agreed on pilot steps and dataset share.

Topics (auto-generated):
- Quantization options (INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ)
- Accuracy regressions and mitigations
- Runtime performance: latency vs throughput, kernel selection
- KV cache behavior with quantized models
- Batching and continuous batching implications
- VPC/on-prem constraints and KMS/HSM integration

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: hey everyone thanks for joining, appreciate you taking the time. we'll do a deep dive on quantization, ravi and i from redwood, and then maya, priya, omar from nebula, right?
[00:10] Dr. Maya Chen: yep thanks lena, excited — we're evaluating quantization to reduce costs on our long-context summarization service, but accuracy is the big worry.
[00:20] Ravi Shah: cool, quick agenda: we cover options (INT8, fp8-ish, gptq, awq), show perf/quality tradeoffs, then ops considerations for private/vpc and on-prem. sound good?
[00:30] Priya Patel: yep, please — and we'll note the specific models, we're on an open 32B transformer variant, mostly 4k-16k context runs.
[00:40] Ravi Shah: perfect. so first, INT8 — it's the most mature from a runtime standpoint. good throughput gains, mature kernels on A100/H100, uses 8-bit matmuls and usually fp16 accumulate. the caveat is symmetric quantization can cause accuracy regressions especially on outlier weights and attention layers.
[01:05] Dr. Maya Chen: when you say regressions, how big are we talking? 1%, 5%? worst-case?
[01:12] Ravi Shah: it depends — for generation-style tasks like yours, we've seen anywhere from <1% to up to 7% drop on rouge/semantic metrics for naive per-tensor INT8. but with per-channel scaling and outlier-aware calibration, you often bring that to under 1.5% on most workloads.
[01:30] Omar Ruiz: hmm what's the calibration cost operationally? we can't run huge calibration jobs on prod.
[01:36] Ravi Shah: calibration can be done on a small representative corpus — 1k to 5k samples often enough. runtime doesn't need the calibration step, it's offline. the pipeline we recommend: run small calibration, evaluate on your 10k holdout.
[01:52] Priya Patel: ok that sounds reasonable. what about fp8? i've read fp8 provides similar speed ups but fewer accuracy issues?
[01:58] Ravi Shah: fp8 (like E4M3/E5M2 formats) can be a nice middle ground: it retains dynamic range and tends to have fewer accuracy regressions, especially on attention and layernorms. but kernel support is more limited — H100 has fp8 native support and specialized kernels; A100 less so. also runtime libraries and ecosystem for fp8 are still evolving.
[02:20] Dr. Maya Chen: and GPTQ/AWQ? we've heard positive things about GPTQ for post-training quantization with minimal quality loss.
[02:28] Ravi Shah: yep GPTQ is post-training, per-channel, and does a good job preserving quality because it optimizes for the reconstruction error per-layer — so you're often seeing near FP16 quality at 4-bit or 8-bit in many cases. downside: it can be compute intensive to run the quantization pass and the resulting runtime sometimes needs custom kernels. AWQ (adaptive weight quantization) is similar idea but focuses on weight outliers and uses adaptive schemes to keep critical weights at higher precision. AWQ often gives an even better quality/size tradeoff on LLMs with outliers.
[03:05] Priya Patel: so would you recommend GPTQ/AWQ over standard INT8 for our use case?
[03:12] Ravi Shah: for quality-sensitive generation — yes, start with GPTQ/AWQ on a small model slice and test on your eval set. for latency-critical endpoints where we need guaranteed kernels and scheduler support, optimized INT8 is lower risk. so sometimes we do a hybrid: production endpoints use INT8 with per-channel and outlier fixes; experimental or high-quality endpoints run GPTQ/AWQ.
[03:35] Lena Park: to add — Redwood's runtime can route requests to different model variants (quantized vs base) depending on policy; that helps with staged rollouts.
[03:45] Omar Ruiz: interesting — how does quantization interact with the KV cache? our workloads use long-lived sessions, we rely heavily on KV caches to reduce compute.
[03:55] Ravi Shah: great question. KV caching is mostly orthogonal but with caveats: if your kv tensors are stored in quantized format to save memory, you need dequantize/requantize paths during generation which can add micro-latency. we usually keep KV cache in a higher precision (fp16) to avoid repeated quant/dequant noise, unless you're extremely memory constrained. also warming the cache matters more with quantized kernels because cold start path can expose quantization noise in early tokens.
[04:25] Priya Patel: so keep KV in fp16, quantize weights — that the recommendation?
[04:29] Ravi Shah: yes, that's the common approach: quantize weights (INT8/GPTQ/AWQ), keep KV in fp16, and if you need memory reduction, use hybrid: quantize non-critical layers and keep attention/cross-attention in fp16.
[04:44] Dr. Maya Chen: what's the impact on latency — our SLA is p95 < 350ms for 2k seq with batch size 1.
[04:51] Ravi Shah: on A100/H100 with optimized INT8 kernels and tuned batch settings, we see token-latency improvements of ~20-35% compared to fp16 for comparable throughput. GPTQ/AWQ runtimes depend on kernel maturity — sometimes similar to INT8, sometimes a small overhead due to packing/unpacking. fp8 on H100 can be even faster but again kernel availability is the gating factor. hitting p95 < 350ms for 2k with batch 1 is feasible but depends on sequence length distribution, batching tail, and whether you do streaming.
[05:20] Omar Ruiz: if we go on-prem, what's the checklist? we run DGX with H100s, NFS storage, internal KMS.
[05:28] Ravi Shah: good — H100 is ideal for fp8 and INT8 kernels. checklist: ensure CUDA/cuBLAS/cuDNN stacks are the recommended versions; install Redwood's runtime package packaged for on-prem; configure Private control plane connectivity (we support air-gapped with hosted licensing); KMS integration for model keys (we support vault and cloud KMS and HSMs); set up network egress rules for telemetry if you opt-in. also confirm NVLink setup for multi-GPU large model sharding.
[05:58] Priya Patel: network egress is a blocker for us, we prefer no external calls from our cluster. is there an offline mode?
[06:04] Lena Park: yes we have an offline/private deployment where the control plane can operate inside your VPC and you can disable telemetry; we provide compliance docs and an install bundle.
[06:12] Dr. Maya Chen: coming back to accuracy regressions — what mitigations are standard if we see a 3-5% drop?
[06:19] Ravi Shah: tactics: 1) per-channel quantization and outlier clipping, 2) mixed-precision layers (keep critical layers in fp16), 3) use GPTQ/AWQ to preserve reconstruction error, 4) fine-tune the quantized model (quant-aware fine-tuning) on a small labeled set, 5) calibration and smarter scaling strategies. often a combination of these reduces regressions to <1% for many benchmarks.
[06:45] Priya Patel: fine-tuning quantized models — is that supported in-redwood or do we need to run offline?
[06:51] Ravi Shah: currently that's outside the managed path; you run quant-aware fine-tuning offline and then upload the checkpoint. Redwood's model onboarding supports custom artifacts and we can help with a runbook. we're working on tighter hooks for quant-aware workflows.
[07:05] Dr. Maya Chen: let's talk numbers — can you share rough perf/quality tradeoff we might expect for our 32B model?
[07:12] Ravi Shah: rough ballpark (very workload dependent): fp16 baseline throughput X, latency baseline Y. INT8: ~1.8-2.2x throughput, 20-35% latency reduction; quality drop naive up to 5% but with per-channel/outlier <1.5%. GPTQ/AWQ 4-bit/8-bit: 2.5x or more throughput in some ops, near-fp16 quality in many cases. fp8 on H100: similar or better than INT8 for latency, with smaller quality delta.
[07:42] Omar Ruiz: you mentioned specialized kernels — how mature are the runtime kernels for GPTQ/AWQ?
[07:48] Ravi Shah: GPTQ has a few community and vendor kernels; Redwood has internal optimized kernels for common GPTQ layouts but for some custom variants you may need additional engineering. AWQ is newer, kernel coverage is growing. In all cases we recommend a small pilot to validate kernel maturity on your GPU/driver stack.
[08:06] Priya Patel: any gotchas with batching? we use continuous batching in prod.
[08:11] Ravi Shah: continuous batching helps throughput but increases tail latency. quantized kernels often have different optimal batch sizes (sometimes larger) because memory footprint is smaller. also dynamic batching with long contexts can create memory fragmentation if KV is stored in fp16 while weights are quantized — watch out for unexpected OOMs. Redwood's runtime has heuristics to pick batch and KV placement but you'll want to tune with your actual workload.
[08:37] Dr. Maya Chen: what's the recommended pilot plan?
[08:40] Lena Park: propose: 1) Nebula provides 10k representative prompts and target metrics, 2) Redwood runs an initial GPTQ and INT8 pass on a subset (1k), shares benchmarks (latency, throughput, quality), 3) run a 2-stage pilot: INT8 in canary path for latency-critical endpoints and GPTQ/AWQ for quality-critical endpoints.
[09:00] Priya Patel: timeline?
[09:02] Lena Park: we can deliver the initial benchmark spreadsheet in 2 business days after we get samples. full pilot 2-3 weeks depending on queues.
[09:10] Omar Ruiz: any security documentation we should review?
[09:13] Lena Park: yes will share SOC2/ISO docs, private deployment whitepaper, KMS integration guide.
[09:18] Ravi Shah: also one quick note on model fallbacks — we recommend a fallback policy for critical inferences: if quantized path fails quality checks, route to fp16 model to avoid user-facing regressions. Redwood supports policy-based routing.
[09:32] Dr. Maya Chen: good — that's important.
[09:35] Priya Patel: a couple of edge questions: 1) do we need to change our prompt structure for quantized models? 2) is function calling impacted?
[09:44] Ravi Shah: 1) prompts generally unchanged; quantization doesn't change tokenization or prompt semantics. but watch for hallucination increases if quality drops — test prompts that probe long-range dependencies. 2) function calling not impacted at the API layer, but downstream latency for streaming function results may change slightly.
[10:00] Lena Park: ok let's wrap — recap and next steps.
[10:03] Dr. Maya Chen: thanks, useful discussion.
